title: Cell Potential, Free Energy and K
short: ΔG° = −nFE°, so a positive E° means a favored reaction with K > 1.
trouble: Students use the wrong n, such as the electrons in one half-reaction before the two were balanced.

blocks.html: A cell's voltage, ΔG° and $K$ all measure how far a reaction wants to go, so each can be computed from the others. Standard potentials are often the easiest of the three to look up.

$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_\text{cell}$, where $n$ is the moles of electrons transferred in the balanced equation and $F = 96\,485\ \text{C/mol}$. Combined with $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$: $\ln K = \dfrac{nFE^\circ}{RT}$, or at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$, $\log K = \dfrac{nE^\circ}{0.0592\ \text{V}}$.

Electrical work is charge times voltage. Moving $n$ moles of electrons (charge $nF$) through a potential difference $E$ can do $nFE$ joules of work, the most useful work the reaction can give, which is $-\Delta G$. Setting the two expressions for $\Delta G^\circ$ equal gives $RT\ln K = nFE^\circ$. At 298 K, $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.0592\ \text{V}$.

blocks.name: ch-cell
blocks.cap: The zinc–copper cell at standard conditions: 1.10 V, which means a ΔG° of −212 kJ and an enormous K.

blocks.title: Zinc and copper
blocks.q: For $\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \to Zn^{2+} + Cu}$, $E^\circ = 1.10\ \text{V}$. Find $\Delta G^\circ$ and $K$ at 25 °C.
steps: Two electrons move per zinc atom: $n = 2$.
$\log K = \dfrac{(2)(1.10)}{0.0592} = 37.2$, so $K = 10^{37.2} = 1.5 \times 10^{37}$. The reaction goes to completion.

blocks.title: Finding n
steps: Aluminum gives 3 electrons, taken by 3 silver ions: $n = 3$.

blocks.title: A small voltage
blocks.q: A one-electron reaction has $E^\circ = 0.10\ \text{V}$. Find $K$ at 25 °C.
steps: $K = 10^{1.69} = 49$. Even a tenth of a volt favors products noticeably.

blocks.html: One consequence of $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$: when two half-reactions are combined into a new half-reaction, potentials do not simply add, because the electrons do not cancel. Add the free energies instead. For example, $\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + e^- \to Fe^{2+}}$ ($+0.77\ \text{V}$) and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2e^- \to Fe}$ ($-0.45\ \text{V}$) give $\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + 3e^- \to Fe}$ with $E^\circ = \dfrac{1(0.77) + 2(-0.45)}{3} = -0.04\ \text{V}$, not $0.32\ \text{V}$.
A large positive $E^\circ$ says a reaction is favored, not that it is fast. Some favored electrode reactions, like making oxygen from water, need extra voltage to run at a useful rate.

Using the wrong $n$, such as the electrons in one half-reaction before the two were balanced, or the number of atoms instead of electrons. Check: write both balanced half-reactions; $n$ is the number of electrons that cancel when you add them.
